title: Your wishes
hookLine: a box ticked at the DMV, and the Buddha telling Ananda what to do with his body
tomorrow: Ông says he isn't afraid of dying. how can that be?

lines: A BOX TICKED AT THE DMV.
cards: At the DMV, people tick a box about organ donation while the clerk waits. For some, that box is the one time anyone asks, out loud, what should happen to their body.

The rest can go unsaid for years, not because people don't care, but because it's hard to start. So how would you want to be cared for at the end? Who should be there, what should be sung, what should be quiet?
Near the end of his life, Ananda asked the Buddha a version of that question, and the Buddha answered it plainly.

teach.h: WHAT SHOULD WE DO WITH YOUR BODY?
teach.b: What should we do with your body, Ananda asks. The Buddha says the monks shouldn't busy themselves with honoring his remains; they should give themselves to the practice.
Lay followers will see to it, and he describes how: the way the body of a great king is honored, and a memorial mound at a crossroads, where people passing can stop and find their minds calmed.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA SAID IT OUT LOUD.
teach.b: The Buddha thought ahead, and he said so out loud, so nobody had to guess. In the same sutta he tells Ananda that after he's gone, the teaching and the discipline he gave will be their teacher. That's the gift in it.

teach.h: WISHES SPARE THE ONES YOU LOVE.
teach.b: Wishes spoken early spare the people who love you from arguing over what you would have wanted. And they turn a frightening subject into a conversation.
Now the week, gathered up. A cave, and seven factors of awakening recited: a chant at the bedside. Two lists, for patient and nurse: care for the carers.
A pot of ghee breaking underwater: the last thought. A Tibetan drill of light: toward the light. One name, held by a vow: the name at the end.
A count in sevens: forty-nine days. And today, a small, practical piece.

how: Buddhist teachers and hospices encourage people to talk with family ahead of time about their wishes for care, chanting and funeral rites; some temples help members write these down.

o: a list of what you'd like to own before you die
saying ahead of time how you'd like to be cared for at the end
the wishes you make while blowing out birthday candles

games.q: the Buddha's answer — tap the pairs.
p: asked what to do with the body
would see to honoring the remains
where passersby find their minds calm

s: the Buddha refused to say what should happen after his death
he answered Ananda plainly: the monks to their practice, lay followers to the remains, a mound at a crossroads.
the Buddha told the monks not to busy themselves with his remains
they were to give themselves to the practice instead.
talking about end-of-life wishes invites bad luck
in the sutta, thinking ahead is a kindness: it spares the people left behind from guessing.

games.q: at dinner, your mom starts to say what she'd want if she were ever very sick. your brother says 'stop, that's morbid.' what fits today's lesson?
o: agree with your brother; it's sad, so it's better left unsaid.
let her finish, and ask a question or two; it's a gift to the family.
change the subject now and plan to write it down for her later.
games.why: the Buddha said his wishes out loud when Ananda asked. spoken early, wishes spare the family from guessing.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write one sentence about how you'd like to be cared for at the end of your life, someday far off: who you'd want near, a song, a quiet room, a chant, a window.
Read it once, slowly, and put it somewhere you'll find it again.

wordCard.voice: Your wishes: saying ahead of time how you'd like to be cared for, as the Buddha told Ananda, so no one has to guess.

orig.note: Pali patthana: a wish or aspiration.

carryVoice: Keep this one: thinking ahead, a kindness to the people who'll be standing there. Twenty-seven of thirty, and a week at the bedside, gathered.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta, ch. 5 (Ananda asks what to do with the Tathagata's remains; monks not to be occupied with honoring them; lay followers will; the king's funeral; a stupa at the crossroads)
